title: Dry-leaf mulch for soil moisture
text: Cover exposed soil around crops with a loose layer of dry leaves or clean crop residue to reduce direct sun and slow moisture loss. Keep material a little away from the stem, check for slugs and rodents, and adjust thickness for local rainfall and crop. For potato, plan planting with the first workable spring soil moisture rather than letting seed tubers sit in dry soil.
source: Nepal hill and mountain farming practice; documented in Khumbu indigenous agricultural knowledge research (2022)
verified_by: Documented in published Nepal research; not a controlled efficacy trial for every crop or location
geographic_scope: Khumbu, Solukhumbu, Nepal; adapt to local altitude and crop
consent_status: Published research reference; no individual farmer attribution used
limitations: Mulch type and thickness depend on crop, slope, rainfall, pest pressure and local availability. Avoid diseased residues.

title: Titepati (Artemisia) as a traditional pest-management plant
text: Titepati is a locally known aromatic plant used in some Himalayan communities as part of traditional pest-management knowledge. Identify the plant correctly before any use. Do not assume a homemade extract is safe or effective on every crop: first consult a local agriculture technician, test a small area, avoid spraying flowers visited by pollinators, and do not apply near harvest without crop-specific guidance.
source: Khumbu, Solukhumbu, Nepal indigenous agricultural knowledge research (2022)
verified_by: Use is documented; preparation, dose and efficacy require crop- and location-specific assessment
evidence_status: DOCUMENTED USE · METHOD NEEDS LOCAL REVIEW
geographic_scope: Khumbu, Nepal; not a universal recommendation
consent_status: Published research reference; no individual farmer attribution used
limitations: No recipe or dosage is supplied because the source does not establish a universal safe formulation. Confirm plant identity and local safety.

title: Selecting and saving local seed
text: Before harvest, mark healthy, true-to-type plants that performed well under your field conditions. Keep seed from those plants separate, dry it thoroughly in shade after initial cleaning, remove damaged or diseased seed, label the crop and season, and store it in a clean, dry, pest-protected container. Exchange local varieties through trusted neighbours or community seed networks while keeping variety names and origin notes.
source: Traditional crop and seed-system research in Nepal, including Kailash Sacred Landscape and mountain seed-system studies
verified_by: Documented farmer practice; seed health and varietal purity depend on crop-specific handling
geographic_scope: Nepal mountain and hill farming systems; adapt to crop and elevation
consent_status: Published research reference; no individual farmer attribution used
limitations: Isolation, drying moisture, storage duration and seed-borne disease controls vary by crop. Use certified seed where disease or varietal purity is critical.

title: Sun-drying grain before storage
text: After harvest, clean grain and dry it well before storage. Spread it in a thin layer on a clean surface, turn it regularly, and protect it from rain, animals and contamination. Store only when it is thoroughly dry in a clean, dry, pest-resistant container; inspect regularly and remove damp or mouldy material promptly.
source: Indigenous agricultural knowledge adoption study, Bhirkot Municipality, Syangja, Nepal (2021)
verified_by: Traditional storage practice documented in Nepal research; safe moisture thresholds vary by grain and storage type
geographic_scope: Bhirkot, Syangja, Nepal; broadly adaptable with crop-specific moisture checks
consent_status: Published research reference; no individual farmer attribution used
limitations: Sun-drying alone does not guarantee safe storage. Avoid re-wetting, monitor insects and mould, and use moisture measurement when available.

title: Bhakari and traditional grain storage
text: Traditional Nepali grain storage includes woven bamboo bhakari structures and hanging maize cobs in clusters. Keep the storage area dry, raised from damp floors, clean and regularly inspected. Only store well-dried grain, repair cracks or gaps, and protect the structure from rodents and rain. Do not rely on traditional coatings alone as a substitute for checking grain moisture and pest infestation.
source: Indigenous agricultural knowledge adoption study, Bhirkot Municipality, Syangja, Nepal (2021)
verified_by: Storage structures documented in Nepal research; performance depends on construction, dryness and maintenance
geographic_scope: Bhirkot, Syangja, Nepal; similar structures vary by community
consent_status: Published research reference; no individual farmer attribution used
limitations: Mustard-cake coating and mud/straw sealing are locally described construction practices, not guaranteed pest control. Ensure food safety and dryness.

title: Mixed cropping and crop diversity
text: Grow compatible crops together where local experience supports it—for example, combine a cereal with a suitable pulse or maintain more than one locally adapted variety across plots. Match plant height, maturity, spacing and water needs so crops do not compete excessively. Keep some seed from different varieties to spread risk, and record which combinations perform well on your own land.
source: Nepal indigenous technology adoption research in Syangja and crop-diversity research in Kailash Sacred Landscape
verified_by: Mixed cropping and on-farm diversity documented in Nepal research; individual combinations need local assessment
geographic_scope: Nepal hill and mountain systems; crop combinations are location-specific
consent_status: Published research reference; no individual farmer attribution used
limitations: No yield increase is promised. Competition, shade, labour and marketability depend on species and planting geometry.

title: Local seasonal indicators for planting decisions
text: Farmers in some Himalayan communities observe flowering of local plants, bird movement, wind, sunlight and familiar seasonal signs when planning field work. Use these observations as supplementary local cues, not as a replacement for rainfall forecasts, soil-moisture checks or crop-specific planting windows. Keep a simple record of the indicator and the actual weather each year to learn whether it remains reliable.
source: Khumbu, Solukhumbu, Nepal indigenous agricultural knowledge research (2022)
verified_by: Indicators documented as local knowledge; predictive reliability varies by place and year
geographic_scope: Khumbu, Nepal; indicator species and timing are location-specific
consent_status: Published research reference; no individual farmer attribution used
limitations: Climate change can shift seasonal timing. Do not use a single natural indicator as a precise weather forecast.

title: Forest-leaf compost and farmyard manure
text: Where locally appropriate and permitted, collect fallen leaves and combine them with farmyard manure and other compostable plant material. Compost the mixture until it is dark, crumbly and no longer heating before applying it to fields. Use only leaves that are safe and locally known for composting; avoid stripping live forest vegetation or collecting from protected areas.
source: Khumbu, Solukhumbu, Nepal indigenous agricultural knowledge research (2022)
verified_by: Leaf resources and animal manure documented as local fertility practices; nutrient content not standardized
geographic_scope: Khumbu, Nepal; local species and livestock systems vary
consent_status: Published research reference; no individual farmer attribution used
limitations: Compost maturity, nutrient content and collection rules vary. Do not harvest live leaves or damage forests.
